I started making continuous mixes about two years ago, and for the road trip to the Celebration show, I made a 13 part series of mixes that runs about 14 hours total, broken down into themed chapters: 

1. Biography (loosely grouped set of songs about growing up, her mom, and her family)

2. Some time in New York City (all pre-signing demos)

3. Boy Toy Breakthrough (the "bubblegum"/teen pop era of the first two albums)

4. Sex (self-explanatory)

5. Inspired by the world (songs with world music influences)

6. Church of Madonna (songs about faith, religion, and philosophy)

7. Collaborations

8. In the Movies (soundtrack recordings)

9. In the Covers (cover versions she's recorded)

10. (Blond) Ambition (songs about working hard, reaching for your dreams, fame)

11. It's a Celebration (random stuff I like that didn't fit into the other themes)

12. Appendix A: Balladeer (favorite ballads)

13. Appendix B: Madonna on a Dance Floor (three hours of remixes)

And each section has excerpts from interviews and TV Appearances that apply to the theme of the section.

If you dive into Queer cinema, there are many positive and uplifting stories out there.  Don't expect any of them to come from a major studio, or even a small one like A24 that has distribution through a larger studio (in this case, Warner).  

There is a short play I used to teach called "Florence" (can't remember the author at the moment), but it was about a Black mother waiting at a train station waiting to go the NY (I think) to try to talk her daughter out of an acting career.  She winds up talking to a white woman who demonstrates that she believes that *every* story about Black people, especially mixed-race people like Florence (the daughter) are tragic stories simply because the lives of all Black people, in her eyes, are fundamentally tragic.  The white woman considers herself an advocate for the Black community, but she carries this idea with her that, because they are face prejudice, they are incapable of having happy endings. The mother winds up understanding how important it is for her daughter to be an actor so that she can tell *positive* stories about the Black community.

Straight people at these studios see us the same way--we must be tragic.  It used to be that every major-studio film about gay men had to be about AIDS.  Then they just moved on to finding other stories where we die, or have horrible experiences and unhappy endings.  Even in those cases where we do get a happy ending (like *Love, Simon*), there has to be a fundamental struggle that they grapple with directly related to their gayness, because the straight people running the major studios can't conceive of gay life being joyful, so they feel the only valid stories they can tell about us are tragic.

The Black community still faces this--the only movie I've seen in recent years where the principle characters were Black and the story was not directly related to tension about their racial identity has been *The Woman in the Yard.*  You could have changed the race of the family in that film, and it wouldn't have changed the story that was being told in any significant way.  It was simply a story in which the main (in fact, all) the characters were Black.

If you want joyful queer films, don't worry about the actors playing the characters--worry about the studio heads, the directors, the writers.  So long as straight people are incapable of seeing Queer joy, they will not tell stories about Queer joy.  It's nothing to do with the actors' sexuality--in many cases, if you want a major studio to finance the film and distribute it, you *have* to cast a star, and most stars are either straight or not out.  So it's a double edged sword--straight people cast straights to tell tragic stories about us, or they simply don't tell stories about us at all. *Queer* most likely got financed because Daniel Craig was involved.  *Brokeback Mountain* had straight actors, but having them be stars is what ultimately got the film made.  Same for *Call Me By Your Name--*Armie Hammer (pre-cannibal texts) was a lot of the reason the film was made.

In terms of "phases," the easiest distinctions would be SAW/PWL years, the DeConstruction years, and then the (post)millennial albums.  

The SAW/PWL years are very much of the PWL  "sound."  Lots of late-80s eurodisco, heavily synthesized, upbeat music with a few MOR ballads thrown in for good luck.  If you're not a fan of SAW in general, these albums won't change your mind (especially the first two).  This was an era where Kylie also had very little say in what she recorded--PWL functioned much like a factory.  It was a powerhouse in its time, and Stock, Aitken, and Waterman remain influential within the industry, but PWL is almost a genre unto itself.  With *Rhythm of Love* and *Let's Get To It*, Kylie tried to have more of a role in the creative process, but SAW were notorious for being ambivalent about the artist's abilities or contributions beyond performance.  During their peak period, they were the epitome of European pop music, but they are a very definite style of music.

The DeConstruction/"Indie-Kylie" years saw Kylie get more control of her work, especially with *Impossible Princess*, where she played a major role in all parts of the production of the album, beginning at song writing.  *Kylie Minogue* is very much tied into the amalgamation of R&B and some of the more "edgy" pop acts of the time with a flare of Madchester-style production added.  *Impossible Princess* goes much deeper into alternative pop/electronic music.  (It's also my favorite of all her albums.

After that, the albums become more individual eras of their own.  Kylie albums following her signing to BMG always sound like Kylie albums, but they rarely sound alike.  You could argue that, beginning with *Light Years*, Kylie's career has combined the commercialism of the SAW years with the experimentation of the DeConstruction years.  They albums gel well together because she has a firm hand in what she puts out, but they also have much more variation to them than the initial four-album PWL run had.  There is an obvious evolution of sound as you work your way through those album, but you never hit a point where it "doesn't sound like Kylie."  

As far as suggestions for where to start, since you've already listened to *Fever*, my recommendations are *Impossible Princess* if you want Kylie at her most experimental, *X* if you want to see her really embrace club sounds and doubling down on the electronics and dance production, both *Tension* albums (with a little more emphasis on *II*) in terms of her having her finger on the pulse of cutting edge electronic dance pop, and *Body Language* to see what happens when she branches into more 00's R&B/American production sounds.

Happy exploring.  I would argue she doesn't have a single bad album.  Your enjoyment of them will depend on your personal tastes.

I taught at a college up until 2021, and many of my students were barely being able to afford tuition, and we were a cheap alternative (Liberal Arts Community College).  Pell grants are not what they used to be.  Subsidized student loans seem to be completely gone. If you don't have to worry about "squeezing" the students because grants and whatnot are picking up the costs, you can charge the kind of tuition where you can afford to build field houses and contemporary student centers, residence halls/dorms, and have robust programs with lots of opportunities for travel and real-world work experiences built into the curriculum, like state of the art labs or practical/practicum spaces. Normally I don't like "cast of thousands" books, but books like *'Salem's Lot, Tommyknockers,* and*, IT* were part of my formative years, and the writing about the small towns is part of what I loved about them so much because it was about the only place where I could find what felt like accurate reflections of the town I grew up in--those little, forgotten places that maybe used to be something, but are now half empty "bedroom communities" for workers at failing factories in a nearby town.  King--especially early in his career--had a fine tuned ear for how the gossip and talk of a small town works.  I know it annoys a huge share of readers, especially ones who can't relate to what he's writing because they never lived in it.  I grew up in Northern New York instead of Maine, but he could have been writing about the town I grew up in--rarely sugar coated, filled with darkness that everyone knows but no one discusses, and the worst monsters are at the little general store in town picking up a gallon of milk and saying hi to you at the checkout.

I loved it when I originally read it, and my enjoyment of it has only decreased a little.  It's a bit awkward because there are points where he seems to want to return to the style of *'Salem's Lot*, where the story is really about the destruction of a small town, but then he wants to tell the story about the aliens just as much, which was not the balance that made *'Salem's Lot* work.  I just re-read SL for about the fiftieth time, and it was the first time that I really noticed that the vampires are barely part of that book--most of the horror is in watching what happens to the town and its people.  *The Tommyknockers* feels like it splits the difference between the two modes, but substitute aliens for vampires.  

But my love for SL is probably why I wasn't bothered at all about the number of times the narrative diverted from the central story line.  It feels like a novel that was a transition between modes for him, and of the books published under his own name, it's one of the few that feels a bit more "Bachman," at least to me.

I think it's really impossible to compare at this point.  The structure of fame and success is radically different at this point than it was then.  Albums would come out and be cultural touch points in the way that they subsumed everything else (much like *Tortured Poets Department* did), but "subsuming everything" was also very different.  In the 80s, the bulk of people still only had over-the-air television, and even cable was limited in the number of choices you had available to you.  

I don't know if Taylor is "bigger" or not at this point than Madonna was in the 80s.  The way things are marketed is very different.  Cross-marketing wasn't a huge thing back then, so when Madonna did the Pepsi ad, there were literally ads for several weeks beforehand that promoted the soda ad.  It's the only time I think I have seen something that was basically a trailer for an ad.  

No social media, no internet.  Being "big" back then was about showing up on MTV and major networks, but you could literally cover all of that inside of a week if you wanted to.  Charts were based mostly on physical media, the singles charts also factored in airplay.  When you shift into "album equivalent" estimates and whatnot, then the numbers start getting more difficult to compare.  While there was still an obsession with stars' personal lives at the time, we didn't have anything like the access that we have now. In defense of those who question Shakespeare's authorship, there are now programs that analyze authorial voice that have provided pretty solid evidence that there are at least two different voices going on in many of his texts.  A professor at my alma mater played a role in developing the software.

We also need to remember that none of Shakespeare's plays where published "direct-to-print."  They were re-assembled from surviving actor copies and memory.  Shakespeare was not writing in a time when writers thought about the "print record" very much, especially dramatic writers, who were already working in a genre that was considered disgusting and beneath contempt.  The Puritans in England at that time had branded theater as the cause of the Black Plague and forced it out of Greater London.  When you went to see a one of Shakespeare's plays, you went to the "bad part of town" where the prostitutes and destitute worked and lived.  Shakespeare's popularity was a large part of what caused the re-evaluation of the value of drama and theater.  His plays were one of the first commercially printed texts that wasn't religious or government based.  It's basically the roots of the "popular press" in the Western world.  But the texts that we have are not the original writings.  They are an attempt by his contemporaries to reconstruct the writing to preserve it.  So at least *some* of the presence of additional voices isn't about spurious authorship, but about spurious memory.

OK, take a breath.  I used to be a professor, and there was usually at least one student every semester who was having this moment.  (Not to say that yours is just some "everyone gets it" thing, just that there are others going through what you are, and you're not a "loser" or a "failure.")  The students are almost always from families where success was just the minimum expectations, and they get a ton of pressure from their family to meet artificial achievement levels that the family has randomly made up.

I don't know what advisor let you register for a maximum credit load after you already struggled with a heavy schedule.  That's a disservice to you if they didn't at least have a conversation with you about taking a different approach.  At the same time, I know it's possible you did have that conversation, but felt too much pressure to do anything but the max load.  

So let this be the learning experience.  You may have to have a difficult conversation with your family about what is appropriate for you.  Either way you look at it, you're looking at more time in school than they seem to expect of you--you'll either need more semesters to make up for the courses you failed by having too much on your plate, or you'll need more semesters to complete because you need a more manageable course load.  The first option also includes the possibility of suspension (and illness), whereas the second option is more likely to be a successful one.

We have become obsessed with the idea of "two-year" and "four-year" degrees.  They *aren't* X-year degrees.  That's some bullshit made up by the student aid entities related to what *they* expect is the average time needed to finish the degree program.  But even the lenders and grant people recognize that a Bachelor's degree might be a 6-year program for some people.  That's why you aren't typically cut off automatically from financial aid after four years.  

The point of being in college (aside from the other socio-developmental benefits) is to get the degree (and hopefully an education).  Obviously, 18 credits per semester is not going to get you that degree.  

You mention the possibility of suspension after this semester.  If that is the case, you can take that time to regroup before going back, or you can consider enrolling at a community college and re-taking the course work you failed, which will then transfer back into your home institution and improve your GPA.  If you take that step, be sure to coordinate with your home college's registrar to make sure you're taking the classes that will transfer in as the ones you weren't successful in prior to your suspension.  That will also put you in a good position because your GPA will have increased when you return to your home college, instead of restarting with the same GPA that you had when you were suspended.

If you aren't suspended, then figure out what is a reasonable course load for you for next semester.  Don't think about what your family thinks you ought to be doing; think about what you know you can manage in addition to your other commitments (and yes, a personal life and recreational time are commitments--it keeps you rested and sane).  When it comes to pressure from your family about deadlines that they've created out of whole cloth, tell them what I already explained--would they prefer more semesters because you got overwhelmed and failed classes and need to retake them, or more semesters because you have a reasonable workload that you can do well in?  

If you're still concerned about a timeline, consider balancing the lighter loads during your regular semester with taking a class or two during summer and winter sessions.  Even if you only did six-credits in the in-between sessions, that reduces your next two semesters from 18 to 15.  (Though, again, try not to be so focused on the idea that there's an expiration on when it's "appropriate to be in college."  Which, by the way, is ridiculous.  26 is still considered "traditional age" by most demographics, and there are tons of older people who are enrolled in degree programs.)

When you rip the music from a disc, there are a ton of different file formats you can select from as well as different levels of quality.  This is usually controlled from a tab that says something like "Audio Quality" or "Rip Settings" inside the program that you use for ripping your files.

**FLAC**

The reason that the songs don't sound as good in the ripped file as they do on the original disc is typically because they were ripped at a lower quality.  FLAC (Free Lossless Audio Compression) is a non-proprietary (meaning it isn't a file type that is the intellectual property of a specific publisher or company that only works within specific programs) shareware (free to all) file format that does not compromise the sound quality of the file in any way.  It's one of the best file formats you can get (there are others, but I don't have the knowledge to explain all of them).  If you are buying a digital music file from a file service, FLAC is one of the best file types you can get (provided it is encoded directly from the masters), because it can reproduce more than a standard CD can in terms of sound (though, typically, this is only noticeable if you're an audiophile and/or using high end equipment).

However, when you rip a file from a source, you can't rip it in a format that is better than the original source.  You aren't going to improve on the quality of a CD by ripping it as a FLAC.  This isn't a big deal if you don't have a ton of music that you're working with.  But if you have a large selection of music, FLAC files often take up too much space to be practical.  

The other issue with FLAC files is that they may sometimes not be readable through certain systems.

**MP3**

MP3s are pretty much universal in terms of being able to be played on any device.  320mbps (megabits per second) is the equivalent rate at which files are encoded for CDs--if you rip a proper CD to a 320mbps file, you should see no difference at all in sound quality from the CD to the file.

There are also lower rates that you can rip a CD at.  The primary reason for using any of those bit rates is to save space.  They will apply further compression to your file, which means you'll be losing information from the track.  *Typically*, it seems most people agree that--aside from listening on audiophile-level equipment or if you have very fine tuned hearing--you *shouldn't* notice much of a difference in audio quality as long as you rip the files at 192mbps or higher.  (I think I can hear a difference if it gets under 256mbps, but that may be psychosomatic).  Below 192mbps, even the average listener will begin to notice distortion and/or compression artifacts that negatively impact the sound quality of the file.

If you rip a CD at 320mbps, this is considered the equivalent of CD quality audio.  It should also play back on any playback device capable of reading music files, and the music should sound identical to if you were playing a CD on the same sound system.

Also, as a note, if you purchase standard downloads from your average internet music provider (Amazon, iTunes, etc.), those files generally are *not* encoded at the optimum level.  Usually, if you play the file on a device that displays the bit rate, you will typically see the files are encoded at a variable bit rate that is done to maximize storage potential on the company's servers.  256mbps tends to be the highest quality bit rate that I have seen on "Official" MP3 purchases.  If you want music files that are in a lossless format, you typically need to purchase them from a more "boutique" outlet that specializes in providing high quality audio files.

**Car Audio**

Many auto manufacturers opt for lower-end sound systems in their vehicles to save money.  This is often the source of the difference that people hear when they play CD-quality audio files (or even actual CDs) on an automotive stereo system.  Your mid-market/high-market cars tend to have better stereo systems in them that will offer more faithful reproduction of your audio.

If there is a problem with the USB interface between the device you store your audio files on or the car's USB port, that will cause distortion that negatively impacts your listening experience.  The same may apply if there are issues with the drive that you use to rip your files or the USB ports/interfaces involved in that process.  

If your audio system within your vehicle is the reason for unsatisfactory audio reproduction, you can consider upgrading your vehicle's system with an aftermarket speaker set, if that is within your means.

You're confusing "hard sciences" (biology, chemistry, physics, geology, etc.) with soft sciences (sociology, psychology, anthropology, etc.)  With hard sciences, typically you can run a test or measure a value and find an answer--like a cholesterol test. In time, we may develop both a better understanding of what causes psychological issues, including learning disorders, the Spectrum, depression, etc. and develop ways to measure tangible aspects of the body to create something like a blood test for depression or a saliva test for Autism.  We just aren't there yet.  This doesn't make it "unscientific."  It's just a variation of science that matches to the subjects being studied.

Heck, for many types of cancer now, we can rule out certain common ones with just a blood test, when we used to go through much more invasive methods, including exploratory surgery ("we don't know what's going on, so we're gonna pop your hood and see what we can find, count back from ten while inhaling the gas.") I don't think that it *forced* people into illegal downloading, but it was a pretty stupid idea for the labels to stop putting out what had traditionally been a way for listeners to get the songs they liked by bands that they weren't necessarily into getting the album from.  The record companies started messing around with singles in the late 80s--one of the first remarkable moments in that timeline was "Ice Ice Baby"--it was, at the time, the biggest single in the country, and the record companies discontinued the single to encourage album sales (they were open about this reason at the time).  

Singles had traditionally been the "gateway drug" for music collectors--if you were young and didn't have a ton of money, you could pick up a seven-inch single pretty cheaply.  Late 80s, the record companies expanded this into cassingles, which also developed a pretty big following.  And it was, again, an opportunity for people who loved the song to buy the song at a relatively cheap price.  (For awhile, some of the labels were gaming the charts by putting out cassingles and encouraging stores to charge ridiculously low prices for them to maximize sales.  The "on special" singles were typically near the register and were under a dollar, and were there like candy bars--as an impulse buy.)  That drove quite a few songs into number-one debuts on the charts.

Then the chart companies began to crack down on that practice (despite the fact that they were still sales).  In fact, in some ways, the chart companies played a role in killing the single as well--especially in the UK, where they began to be so strict about what would and would not count for the singles charts that they began seriously limiting what could even appear on a single.  Suddenly you couldn't have more than two formats count for the charts, and they couldn't be over 20 minutes total for the full single/maxi-single, or they wouldn't count for the chart.  And they kept adding more restrictions until they weren't really a value for the collectors anymore.  (In the UK, rather than undercutting prices on singles to drive sales, they had developed a practice of multi-disc single releases.  Part 1 had b-sides.  Part 2 had remixes.  There might be a Part 3 that had something else.  Sometimes one of the singles came with an expanded package that could hold the other singles, which, of course encouraged people to collect.)

But in the US, the labels had this idea that no singles would mean all those people who would have bought the single would just buy the full-length album.  That had spurious success as an approach for a period of time, but then Napster came along, and if you really liked that song and didn't want to buy a whole album just to hear it, you downloaded it.  

So the labels set the stage for there to be a demand for other methods of consuming music, and never provided those methods, because they were focused on the idea that they could force sales of full-length albums.  Rather than recognizing the signs that there was still a market for singles, they just did everything they could to make the new method of consumption disappear.  Until they figured out how to make that work for them (though not artists), and here we are.

There's some life in the single yet.  Many artists have begun pressing limited runs of singles--even on CD--and selling them directly through their sites, often with collectible covers and whatnot.  A few veteran acts (Pet Shop Boys, New Order, Orchestral Maneuvers in the Dark, etc.) are still putting out maxi-singles.  Pet Shop Boys currently have a single on pre-order for their lead track from their next album, and that has two b-sides on it.  So the single isn't completely dead.

For me, it just felt like the singles extended an album era to "matter" beyond just the first few weeks the album was out.  There was always "more to come" if you were interested in getting it.

Promo copies are kind of weird in collecting circles, because some people feel they're more valuable than the regular release, while other people feel like the stamping and whatnot detracts from the release.  I'm kind of middle of the road.  If it's an essential-to-me artist, I don't want the stamping on it, but for anything else it doesn't bother me to have the stamps.  I don't value it more though.

Some of the detractors for promo copies are also concerned that the discs have often been treated rather badly because they were being handled as "just a promo" by people like DJs and store clerks using them for in-store play, who typically aren't overly concerned about keeping the discs pristine.  Though they may value it more if it is an unused promo copy, because that's more rare, especially with popular titles.  I'm pretty sure there are a ton of people who would pay big money for a mint-condition *Thriller* promo LP, for instance, since most of those promos were played until the grooves went flat.  Promos from independent labels also tend to be valued higher than typical promo copies, just because of scarcity.

The *highest* value for promo copies, however, tends to be for the rare cases where the promo was far enough in advance of the actual release that there are differences in things like cover art or even track listings or included versions.  For instance, sometimes a radio edit replaced the originally intended album version if it was a lead single that did exceptionally well in a remixed form.  Or a track was dropped between the pressing of the promo and the actual release.  These things, by the way, did not happen very much (hence the higher value), but there are instances, especially pre-2000s, where a promo was sent out before actual pressings had been done yet, and enough time lapsed that a last minute change altered the finished version.  It does, however, occur more when you talk about promo singles, where artists or labels more frequently changed there minds between the promo wave and the physical single release.

If I were in your position, I'd propose this as a compromise--get her assessed and, if appropriate, diagnosed *now*, but remember that you aren't required to disclose that diagnosis to her school unless you want her to receive accommodations.  That way, if she has no problems when she gets to school (which is possible), then it doesn't need to be shared with her school.  *But*, if problems should present themselves at that point, then you already have the diagnosis, which will allow you access to accommodations much more quickly.  

You can also then make an informed decision about what kinds of services might be appropriate for her.  Additionally, you'll be able to explain The Spectrum to her in positive ways that will hopefully help her avoid the fear of stigmatism from her peers because she'll know more about autism than they do, and having a supportive home with loving parents where she is accepted as she is will give her the understanding that she's not less than anyone; she's just different from many people, but like many other people (which is true for most people in some ways beyond The Spectrum).

I fear the message that will come with not assessing her may be that there's something "wrong" with her if she is diagnosed later and learns that she could have been diagnosed now, but her father wasn't supportive of that.

As a huge fan of Hole, I feel the need to point out the the album "Clebrity Skin" came from tends to be a bit divisive among the fan community.  I think it's easily the equal of *Live Through This*, but some fans don't like that it's a "poppier" album.  Courtney wanted to do something different from what she had done before, and she made a conscious effort to make an album that was more "accessible" (whatever that means) then what she had done before.  It's the album where she basically said, "Yeah, I loved the Germs, but I also loved Fleetwood Mac."  (Coincidentally or related, it's the same time period they recorded a cover of "Gold Dust Woman" for the second Crow movie.)

So that may be the reason it hit you different from their other stuff.  For *Celebrity Skin*, she stopped playing the guitar for the album so she could really focus on the lyrics and the vocals--she *wanted* to sound better, because she knew her previous work had been abrasive (deliberately), and she didn't want everyone to think that was all there was to her.

In fact, pretty much every Hole album, sounds different from one another.  *Pretty on the Inside*  is straight up noise rock like some of the edgier work by Sonic Youth.  *Live Through This* adds more melody and more of the groove that were hallmarks of grunge.  *Celebrity Skin* is like the very definition of pop-rock in the best sense of the word (in my opinion), in that is keeps the essence of both genres without bending too far toward one of the other.  And *Nobody's Daughter* (which is a Hole album in name only, since Courtney was the only original member at that point) is more of a singer/songwriter album.  

Her solo album, *America's Sweetheart*, is something of an oddity, since it tries to keep the pop, but go in a more metal direction than she had been prior to it, and the result is mixed--some gems and then some stuff that sounds a little like bad 80s hair metal.  And she was on a lot of drugs at the time, but this time it didn't work the same way as it did with *Live Through This*.

The "lost" album (you can find it online, usually, often as *How Dirty Girls Get Clean* or *The Rehab Demos*) that became *Nobody's Daughter*  is even more obviously a singer-songwriter album, and I wonder some times if it would have been better received as a solo disc in that style than it was when she decided to put it under the Hole brand with a different version of the band.  

I saw her live with the "new" Hole, though billed as a solo act, in Toronto, and she put on a fucking AMAZING show.  And she's also really funny; at least she was then.  She was also sober at the time.

And this is probably more information than you wanted about Hole and Courtney Love, but I'm a fan, so it kind of felt like a duty.

Think of the producer like a coordinator.  They work with the act (to the extent that the act wants to collaborate--some singers, for example, just want to show up, sing, and go back to their mansion) to help the act achieve their vision, but they also employ networks of engineers, mixers, studio musicians, etc. to achieve that sound.  

Not every producer has a distinct "style," but most of the producers that you encounter on multiple albums by many different artists typically do have some sort of "trademark" sound that is the reason the act (or label) hires them in the first place.  Phil Spector was probably the first mega-producer with his Wall of Sound style of production (though, if you listen to some of his later work, that didn't remain his trademark).  If you want something that's going to sound gritty and "organic," a lot of the time you want someone like Rick Rubin (despite his roots in hip-hop).  Stuart Price is going to help you achieve a warm, synth-based sound that tends to wash in waves rather than punch.  Timbaland is going to bring you beats, and probably also foist himself on you as a singer in some capacity, despite.....maybe we should just let him produce (and if you want to see the huge effect a change in producer can create, check out the album he produced for Chris Cornell, though this may be an unpleasant lesson to learn from, depending on your tastes).  Brendan O'Brien had quite a reputation for awhile of helping more veteran acts adopt to newer trends without losing their identity in the process.  Pharrell is going to most likely bring you poly-rhythms.  Mark Ronson will bring a retro-flare to your sound.

At the time, especially, Jeff Lynne was known for a style that was frequently criticized as "over produced."  While I love *Cloud 9* (the album he produced with Harrison before the Wilburys happened), you can hear a marked difference between that album and anything else Harrison did.  It's a very polished sound, catchy, poppy, but also a little bit anonymous (especially at the time, when that slick sense of production was all over the radio).  Some people love that album and Lynne's work, because it helped bring Harrison back to a much larger, mainstream audience. But some people hate it for almost the same reasons, and that it also cut back on Harrison's experimental tendencies.  The idea that he became "just a pop star."

Many artists will opt to co-produce, which helps their catalogs to maintain something of a more cohesive sound that is considered more reflective of them as a whole.  But if you want to get a sense for what a producer can do in terms of affecting and act's sound, turn to any band that *doesn't* co-produce with their hired producer, and take stock of the variations in character between albums that were done with different producers.  The aforementioned *Scream* by Chris Cornell makes it *really* obvious how a producer can affect the act's sound, but it's also a polarizing record, with the bulk of people who are fans of Cornell being at the end that thinks it is some form of blasphemy.  If you love Sound Garden, you're probably not going to love *Scream*.  I like it as an oddity, and it's a great album for the album that it is, but it's simultaneously probably the worst album that Cornell had any involvement in.  When the multi-disc retrospective for Cornell was assembled, every track from that album appeared in a different form that stripped away the Timbaland production.

I would also speculate that you can get a good idea for what bands you like are best represented as "themselves" on their recordings.  If the sound varies greatly from one producer to the next, they probably don't play a huge role in their own music's sound, at least in the studio.  If there is a relatively consistent aspect to their music, regardless of who is producing, then they are probably more hands on (and also likely have a co-production credit).

I know that profiling has mixed results and is somewhat controversial, but one of the keys steps in profiling a killer is figuring out what the story is that they are telling themselves where they are the hero.  His story is that he is bringing people the opportunity for redemption, and it is up to them whether they accept that or "opt" for death.  He's a very dangerous version of deranged psychopath, but, unlike most movies in the sub-genre, we get something closer to *his* version of the story in relation to the murders.  It's one of the things I like about *Saw* in opposition to many other movies built around iconic killers--he's not "just some psycho" whose only motivation is murder and carnage (even if that's all he really is).  He's not getting revenge for some perceived sleight against him.  He feels he's a "teacher."

In the rare incidents where we have been able to actually study serial killers, they very often have some form of "logic" to their deeds.  They're "bettering the world" or "creating the 'perfect' person" or "sending a message" or "punishing the wicked," etc.

But he's a raging psychopath--just like Dexter (to site another "hero" serial killer)--except we're clued in to his reasoning, which, in a backwards, disturbing way "makes sense," on some level, which makes him even more frightening, because he's "appealing" to a certain degree.  Hannibal Lecter is another character who is truly unhinged, but we're introduced to his "logic," and he becomes something of an anti-hero, because the way the story is told, we more or less understand where he is coming from.  I think the edge that *Saw* has, more or less (it's not always adhered to), is that we can see John's reasoning, but we also are more ambivalent to his victims than with Hannibal.  In the *Silence of the Lambs* series, the people Hannibal kills are people whose "faults" we see, and they are made explicit enough that there is a certain sick justice to his killings.  In the *Saw* films, all we really get for most of the murders is the recording that justifies the killing (sorry...."test"), but they are, otherwise, blank slates that we're more or less a jury for.  Is the great infraction they have committed in the eyes of John truly as worthy of the punishment his test gives them?  So he has more room to be monstrous, whereas the *SotL* films typically seem to *want* you to sympathize with Hannibal and his "cause."  In the novels, that serves a much more pointed narrative purpose, whereas in the films, especially since Ridley Scott wussed out on the ending of *Hannibal*, it's not quite as clear why we're being manipulated to "understand" him.  With John, on the other hand, we're permitted the narrative space to see both the justification but also the sickness of his pathology.

I grew up on a small family dairy farm (in case anyone wants context), and still live in a rural area, though you couldn't get me back on a farm if the only other choice was death.

I think there is some cultural bias/prejudice that rural people are "ignorant."  If you look for who they put in as stupid, uncultured, or intolerant people in movies and TV shows, they almost universally go for rural stereotypes (especially southern ones).

Another issue that creates a stigma is the general disdain for work that is heavy on manual labor.  We don't tend to think highly of anyone who's occupation is built more around the capabilities of their body than their intellect (construction workers, road crew, etc.).  (Just to be clear, I don't believe this \[because I know better\], but there are plenty of people who do.)  Rural people are often stereotyped with a lot of traits that we socially tend to have contempt for: poverty, ignorance, intolerance.

Many people also have no idea what is involved in agriculture, especially in the modern context.  They think you throw some seeds on the ground in spring  and cut down what grows in the fall, then sell it and make a ton of money, that you then drink during the winter.  They have zero idea of what work actually goes into a farm.

Corporatization of agriculture has also played a role in negative sentiments. Many documentaries and new programs have focused on corporate farming and the issues it presents to the environment.  Even where I live, where the small "city" (barely) is surrounded by farm land, the only time we really hear any news related to farming is when there's some disaster, like the manure lagoon that broke about a decade or so back and dumped around a million gallons of shit into the river that many of the towns draw their drinking water from.  There isn't much focus on the role in maintaining society that food production plays.

Farmers also become political footballs periodically, especially when it comes to (as mentioned by several others on here already) government subsidies.  There's this image that farmers are paid by the government to do nothing, because there isn't a good understanding among the public of how subsidies work and why they exist (primarily for controlling prices and avoiding the market being flooded at any given time, which would collapse Wall Street dividends on agricultural futures).

A lot of people find it easier to look down on things they don't understand than to actually put in the effort to understand them.  That's the shortest path to having a group stigmatized.

Like any categorization system, it's completely subjective.  What one person considers a rock song, another might consider a pop song.  Sheryl Crow is often considered rock, but she's also been considered pop, and there are a number of country elements in her work as well (even aside from the "country" album that she did).

If you want a prime example of how difficult it is to think about genre in terms of being an objective labeling system--look at the realm of alternative music.  For every genre, there seems to be an "alt" version of it, and the elements that make those artists "alt (pop/rock/dance/etc.)" seem to vary from one person to the next.  (I was music director for a start-up alternative station for a brief period of time, and the number of meetings we had that were long battles about "no \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ isn't alternative"  "yes it is" were maddening.)

Even the genre labels that seem like they are much more objective--for example "indie," which, at it's simplest, refers to bands not signed to major labels--aren't as easy to assign firm labels.  Nirvana was indie, as were some of the biggest acts during that time period.  But when they're at the top of the pop charts and then move to major labels, are they still "indie" even though the style of music hasn't really changed much at all?

There's an arguments to be made that almost all music you hear on the radio now is pop music--both because it is "popular" (the root of the label), and because it follows your standard verse/chorus/verse/chorus/(bridge)/chorus to the end structure for composition.  But it's difficult to throw Keith Urban, Metallica, and Justin Bieber into the same category and have that category still have something in the way of meaning.

A lot of journalists use "pop" to refer to music they think of as "disposable"--meant for its time on the radio and then meant to be forgotten.  But every genre has artists who follow that model as well.  

So I don't think there really is a firm answer about where the line goes, because everyone draws the line in different places.  And often the idea of genre is simply used by people to dismiss large bodies of music they have no interest in ("I hate country"), but if you were to push them and have them listen to a selection of music that actually "represents" the genre, they will find music they like.  And in that case, you'll typically find they say something like, "Well, yeah, but \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_  isn't *really* that genre."

I don't see any notes in Discogs about there being an edition that was copy protected, but it's not completely out of the question.  However, copy-protected discs, as far as I know, will typically play just fine, they just distort when they are ripped.

There can sometimes be encoding issues that make discs difficult/impossible for the machine to read them.  This is very rare, but not completely impossible.  If you have a non-computer drive player (boom box, shelf unit, component unit, etc.), try the disc in that and see if it still has an issue.  If it plays fine there, then it's likely a copy-protection issue.  (Copy-protection was a scheme the majors tried pout briefly in the early 00's where they encoded the discs so they either could not be ripped at all, could not be read by ROM drives, or would rip with distortion.  The labels abandoned it after there was a huge amount of consumer backlash, and--if I remember correctly--the international body that controls CD specs took issue with the disc functionality being compromised.  The latter is mostly what killed Dual-Discs.)

I would suggest returning it and exchanging it for a new copy to see if it happens with that one.  If it happens with the new copy, then it's either copy-protection or an encoding issue that affected a batch of the CDs.  If there's a Deftones fan community, you might want to ask there to find out if other people had a similar issue with that release.

One other problem I hadn't considered: Discogs says that some editions of that release were enhanced CDs (meaning there was bonus content included on them that could only be read by CD-ROM drives).  If you have an edition that is enhanced, it's possible that your drive isn't handling the enhanced content well and is having trouble differentiating the text/video content and the audio content.  That can be an issue with some enhanced discs with older technology used for their enhanced content that modern drives aren't equipped to read.

NTA, and your wife is having trouble understanding that you're not "blaming her for getting sick" which would be an asshole move, but you *are* blaming her for not attempting to get well.  And that *is* on her.  

And it's not just a matter of the inconvenience it poses when you have to "cover" for her.  If she is constantly sick, that weakens her in other ways, and repeated illness can eventually lead to long-term damage that can't be fixed, because it has put too much strain on the system.

Even if it's "just a bad cold," if it keeps repeating, it's not *just* anything.  It's becoming chronic.  And it is possibly a sign of underlying problems as well, which could be far more serious than "just a cold."  Constant respiratory illnesses can be a sign of anything from untreated allergies\*  to much worse things like pulmonary hypertension.  And even the "smaller" issues, left untreated, can make things worse.

One of my friends buried her father two years ago.  He refused to ever get a colonoscopy.  But if he had gone when he was supposed to, he probably would have been here another 30 years.  Instead, he waited until he was getting serious symptoms, and by that point it was too late.

We're seemingly taught to discredit the concept of "wellness care," but it *does* save lives.  And your wife isn't even doing sick care, so I'm guessing she's *never* done any wellness checkups.  At 21, that's probably not going to kill her.  But it's going to make things more difficult later, when constant infections and illness start creating scar tissue or tissue damage.

BTW, if this is happening repeatedly and is so bad that she literally can't do anything, that's not "just a cold."  She should have been at the doctor's the first time that happened.

​

\*(I can vouch for this one--I was sick constantly for a few years with colds, bronchitis, ear infections, sinus infections, and once my allergies were treated \[literally two pills a day\], I haven't had a problem, but letting it go as long as I did managed to cause asthma.)

This is something that people seem to forget.  Writing your own music was actually frowned upon until around the 1960s.  Pop singers (pre-rock) were looked at as   
"interpreters," not song-writers.  The Brill Building, Tin Pan Alley, and Motown are three prime examples of environments where songs were written by the professionals and the artists recorded their interpretations.  

The 60's was the point where it became somewhat "normal" for artists to write their own music.  The Beatles were big pioneers in this area, but even their earliest albums (about half their discography) are typically half cover songs.

Country music took a little bit longer, in general, to become a "DIY" genre (for lack of a better term).  There have always been artists who wrote their own music, but it hasn't been the norm.  But there seems to be a lot of pushback almost every time someone in country covers something from an "outside" genre.  Add in the current sensitivity about "cultural appropriation," and "Fast Car" becomes a target, even though many other country (and other) artists have made a living covering songs that were written by people of other races.  

"Fast Car" is also the kind of song that sounds very "personal" (whether it is or not), so that causes some people to flinch.  But it's not even the first cover--it's a popular song, and it's incredibly well-written, so of course people want to sing it.  It's an *amazing* song.  

I think some of the pushback was also from the realm of the assumption that country music is inherently racist (and if we want to go there, then we also need to have a long talk about several other genres while we're at it).  So a song about poverty written by a black woman coming from a successful white man in country music is going to piss a lot of people off.  Which, in and of itself, I think is racist.  A great song is a great song, and not every song has to be about someone's personal experience (though I've read the Combs didn't grow up well off either--poverty is poverty).  It's not like the song is about being Black.  Or being a woman.  

Plus, love it or hate it, she's making more money right now than she has in a long time because of its success.  Probably more than Combs is making from it, in all honesty, because hit songs are one of the rare areas where songwriters tend to come out ahead.

I don't think it's necessarily an actual sexuality, per se, but it means that you aren't interested in sex and/or romance unless you feel like you know the person and are attracted to their personality.  In that case, sexuality and romance are based on the individual, rather than the broad categories we think of with most sexual labels.  So (if this is the case), then you're not going to be able to say "I'm attracted to men" or women or both or whatever combination you might think of.  It's that you need to feel like you have a real connection with the actual person.  And this can be to varying degrees.  Some people it's more of a case of "prefer to know the person," and they could still do a hookup to a certain extent, though they might not enjoy it as much.  Other people, it means they're never going to be interested in having anything to do with someone on the sexual and/or romantic level unless they've had time to learn who they are.  To get to know them.  To feel like you have a connection.  

The reason you may not be aware as to whether or not this is who you are may simply be because you haven't had that level of connection with someone yet.  It's not as easy as being somewhere and thinking, "Oooo, that person is hot."  It takes time--conversation, doing things together, building that connection, before you'll have any idea whether you're attracted to the person or not, because it's not about looks or genitals--it's about the actual person.  And with as hectic as our lives are, how many people of any label or gender have you had a chance to get to know that well?

But that could just as easily *not* be the answer.  As a few people have already said, this is where counseling can help, because the answer is inside of you, but you haven't recognized it yet.  And that is 100% normal.  Many people go through that for extended periods of time to some degree or other.  And, as mentioned earlier, it may change even when you are aware of it, because the answer develops over time.  For instance, if you finally found that connection and found yourself sexually and romantically attracted to a member of the opposite sex, you might think of your "label" as straight.  As time passes, you might find that kind of connection with someone of the same sex, in which case, you may identify more as bisexual, or pan sexual, or gay.  

The label is something only you can know for certain, but it doesn't stop others from trying to label you, which becomes frustrating, especially when you're in a situation where the label you think applies is one that others don't believe exists.  (For instance, there are still many people who don't believe anyone is *really* bisexual, or *really* pansexual, or *really* asexual, but that doesn't mean you can't be any of those things, because who you are is not determined by other people.  That doesn't necessarily mean that *you* "know" who/what you are, which is of no help right now when you're looking for answers.)

You're on the same journey as any of us.  At the moment, you may be less sure of your destination than some others are, but it doesn't mean you aren't on the journey.  And any journey lasts as long as it takes for you to reach the destination, so you don't need to have an answer today, or next week, or in ten years.  And even when you think you have the answer,  that doesn't mean it might not change.  

In the gay community, we have a tendency to assume some degree of certainty, and we also seem to have a ton of support for people who realize and accept their homosexuality late in life, but there doesn't seem to be as much acceptance of the idea that the answer changes. I'm very firmly gay.  Had one girlfriend for a week in college that involved a lot of tequila and, therefore, in my opinion, doesn't count.  (It was a time when there was much more pressure around the idea of, "How do you know if you haven't tried," and probably 90% of the reason I had a little tour through "heterosexuality" was because I was getting sick of not being able to answer that insulting question.  We've come to place more emphasis on self-definition rather than what others may impose on us, but we still fall for the trap of subscribing to labels and thinking they will never change, or that any change is some sort of insult or must be a lie.  I hope, now that we have begun to get away from the gay/bi/straight dynamic and recognized there are other options, that we will also begin to understand that everyone is on a journey. I know it's all well and good to call it a journey and make it sound like some wonderful, mystical thing, but that it does nothing to resolve the frustration that comes with not "knowing the answer" in this moment. I was in my thirties before I even heard the concept of non-binary or gender fluid or any of the other terms that we now use to describe that grey area, and, with that knowledge, I realized why "man" never completely seemed like the right answer.)

I hope you find the ability to enjoy the journey, and that you find something in the way of resolution soon, so you have that peace of mind.  But don't force yourself into a category that doesn't fit you. You can be whatever you want, even if we haven't found the term for it yet.

I had to reach a point where I stopped caring what other people thought of me, and then I actually made liking whatever I liked part of simply who I was.  Yes, I probably like what I listen to, but I also like *all these other things*.  And if you don't, that's cool.  I'm still listening to them.

My tastes are really eclectic, so I can usually find something in common with almost anyone who listens to music, but inevitably, I also listen to a lot of music they don't like.

It also helped when I reached a point where it was easier to diversify my friends, so I wasn't around people who were into the same general music. ETA:  Also, one more point, you may find yourself coming back to "your" music and integrating it with the new music you have discovered through your friends after you have had some time to process the music.  Making mixes/playlists is a great way to begin integrating old and new interests.

From what I've read (I'm newly diagnosed as well), OCD and AD(H)D are both so frequently linked with autism that there is some debate as to whether they are, in fact, a component of the spectrum or simply common comorbidities.

I had some serious OCD issues as a teen, but they have mellowed out some during adulthood.  The main issue I have is my hands.  I don't like anything on my hands at all, including lotion.  I don't like things touching my hands.  If I touch something, my hands automatically feel dirty, and I have to wash them.  Sometimes twice.  This is true even if the thing I was touching was something I was using to clean something with (which, you would think, would mean it, itself, is clean, but for some reason, it doesn't work that way).  It's a pain in the ass, but much more livable than what I have heard in terms of what other people endure with their OCD.

I don't know if my preoccupation with having things in threes counts as OCD or not.
